notes: Disability discrimination and unfair dismissal appeal; Court of Appeal restored ET decision on section 6 reasonable adjustments.

enrichment.short_title: Home Office v Collins: disability discrimination and failed probation dismissal
key_facts: Miss Collins, an insulin-dependent diabetic Home Office administrative assistant, was dismissed after extended probation for poor attendance following stress and depression.
Occupational Health reports indicated she remained unfit to return and might need a phased part-time return in three to six months.
The employment tribunal found no disability discrimination or unfair dismissal; the EAT reversed on justification and failure to make reasonable adjustments.
The Home Office conceded less favourable treatment related to disability but argued dismissal was justified and no section 6 duty arose while she was medically unfit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal allowing Miss Collins's appeal against an employment tribunal dismissal of disability discrimination and unfair dismissal claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the employment tribunal's decision was reinstated and the claimant's complaints dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a disabled employee remained medically certified unfit to work at all, including part-time, an employer was not in breach of section 6 of the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 by declining to offer phased return until a definite return date was known; prolonged absence could justify dismissal on capability grounds with fair procedure.
legal_issues: Whether failure to offer phased or part-time return constituted a breach of the section 6 reasonable adjustment duty
Whether dismissal for failed probation due to absence was justified under section 5
Whether the employment tribunal erred in law in its application of sections 5 and 6
Whether the dismissal procedure was unfair given the minded-to-dismiss letter
linked_authorities: Archibald v Fife Council [2004] UKHL 32
Clark v Novacold Ltd [1999] ICR 951
Post Office v Jones [2001] ICR 805

notes: Short costs judgment on successful contempt appeal; half costs awarded to contemnor.

enrichment.short_title: Symes v Phillips: costs after successful contempt sentence appeal
key_facts: Robin James Symes was committed to prison for two years for contempt; the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to one year.
The contemnor sought costs of the appeal though he did not challenge costs below.
The claimants argued the contemnor brought proceedings on himself and should not recover appeal costs.
Counsel found little authority on costs in successful contempt appeals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for costs following a successful appeal reducing a committal for contempt of court.
enrichment.outcome: The contemnor was awarded one half of the costs of the appeal, including the costs of the costs issue.
enrichment.ratio: While there is no difference in principle between costs in civil contempt and other inter partes proceedings, special factors apply including the contemnor's weaker position to claim costs and the need not to deter claimants who can assist the appellate court; the court may depart from costs follow the event.
legal_issues: Whether costs on a successful contempt appeal follow the ordinary civil appeal rule
What weight to give to the contemnor's admitted contempt and liberty of the subject
Whether claimants who unsuccessfully defended the appeal should pay costs
linked_authorities: Knight v Clifton [1971] Ch 700
Enfield London Borough Council v Mahoney [1983] 1 WLR 749
Harris v Harris [2002] Fam 253

notes: Important Mental Health Act section 139(2) construction; civil proceedings without leave are a nullity.

enrichment.short_title: Seal v South Wales Police: section 139(2) leave and nullity of proceedings
key_facts: Mr Seal brought damages claims against South Wales Police after arrest and section 136 detention without obtaining High Court leave under section 139(2).
A district judge struck out the whole claim as a nullity; the county court judge reinstated non-section 136 parts only.
Mr Seal argued proceedings could be stayed pending retrospective leave; the police argued civil proceedings commenced without leave were void.
The claim was issued at the end of the limitation period after legal aid was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal on whether civil proceedings brought without section 139(2) High Court leave are a nullity or curable by subsequent leave.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; proceedings relating to acts under the Mental Health Act brought without required leave are a complete nullity.
enrichment.ratio: Section 139(2) of the Mental Health Act 1983 uses mandatory language applying identically in effect to civil and criminal proceedings; failure to obtain prior High Court leave renders civil proceedings a nullity rather than a defect remediable by later consent, following Pountney v Griffiths and the section's protective purpose.
legal_issues: Whether section 139(2) is mandatory or directory
Whether proceedings without leave may be stayed pending retrospective leave
Whether civil and criminal consent requirements should have the same consequence
Application of Rendall v Blair and In re Saunders to mental health proceedings
linked_authorities: Pountney v Griffiths [1976] AC 314
Winch v Jones [1986] QB 296
R v Angel [1968] 1 WLR 669

notes: Article 8 immigration appeal; cerebral palsy child case dismissed after Huang and Razgar principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Dbeis v SSHD: Article 8 and removal of child with cerebral palsy
key_facts: A Lebanese asylum seeker and her two sons, including Tarek who has cerebral palsy, sought to remain in the UK on Article 8 grounds after asylum failed.
The adjudicator found adequate medical and educational facilities existed in Lebanon and removal was proportionate.
The IAT applied a Wednesbury-style test rather than evaluating proportionality itself; further medical evidence emerged on appeal.
Expert evidence indicated specialist UK schooling and therapy would not be available in Lebanon.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on Article 8 proportionality after refusal of asylum and human rights appeal, following CA v SSHD jurisdiction limits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; even applying Huang and Razgar correctly, the case was not exceptional enough to override immigration control.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator and, on law-only appeal, the IAT must themselves evaluate Article 8 proportionality rather than ask whether no reasonable Secretary of State could decide; better UK education and therapy for a disabled child does not ordinarily constitute an exceptional case warranting departure from immigration rules.
legal_issues: Correct Article 8 proportionality approach after Huang and Razgar
Whether cerebral palsy amelioration rather than cure affects the analysis
Admissibility of evidence before the IAT under section 101(1)
Whether the IAT's Wednesbury reasoning was an error of law
linked_authorities: Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 105
R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27
CA v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 1165

notes: Case stated on Anti-Social Behaviour Act 2003 dispersal powers; multi-zone locality and reasonable grounds upheld.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v L: dispersal zones and reasonable grounds under ASBA 2003
key_facts: Superintendent House authorised six non-contiguous dispersal zones in South Oxhey under section 30 after anti-social behaviour problems.
PC Hemmings directed six youths including L and N to leave all zones and not return for 24 hours; they re-entered Zone 2.
Youth court magistrates held multi-zone authorisation invalid and that reasonable grounds were insufficient.
The youths had no residence within the authorised locality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case stated from West Hertfordshire Youth Court on preliminary rulings dismissing charges for breach of dispersal directions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; multi-zone non-contiguous localities may be lawful and authorisation plus local knowledge could provide reasonable grounds under section 30(3).
enrichment.ratio: A relevant locality under section 30 may comprise non-contiguous zones if together they sensibly amount to a locality; a constable may exclude persons from all zones and may rely on authorisation and local knowledge, applying O'Hara, without needing particular conduct at the moment of direction.
legal_issues: Whether multiple non-contiguous zones can form one relevant locality
Whether a constable could exclude youths from all six zones
What constitutes reasonable grounds under section 30(3)
Proportionality and civil liberties in use of dispersal powers
linked_authorities: O'Hara v Chief Constable of the Royal Ulster Constabulary [1997] AC 286
R v Westminster City Council, ex p Ermakov [1996] 2 All ER 302

notes: DRC asylum Article 8 appeal dismissed after Huang; wife's ELR not analogical support for proportionality.

enrichment.short_title: Mongoto v SSHD: Article 8 family life and relocation to Kinshasa
key_facts: Mr Mongoto, a credible Congolese human rights activist, claimed asylum after detention and torture; his wife and child had earlier received exceptional leave to remain.
The adjudicator found internal relocation to Kinshasa safe and Article 8 removal proportionate; the IAT applied pre-Huang M (Croatia) Wednesbury reasoning.
The wife had been raped by rebels and granted four years' ELR with a newborn while the appellant remained in detention.
The appellant argued his wife's ELR and family concession policy supported an exceptional Article 8 case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal stayed pending Huang; challenge to IAT dismissal of asylum and Article 8 appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; even under Huang the facts were not truly exceptional and analogical reliance on the wife's ELR was rejected.
enrichment.ratio: After Huang, an adjudicator must decide whether an Article 8 case is truly exceptional rather than applying Wednesbury deference; compassionate ELR granted to a spouse does not create enforceable expectations or analogical support for the appellant, and safe relocation to Kinshasa with family undermines exceptional family separation.
legal_issues: Effect of Huang on IAT Article 8 review
Whether wife's exceptional leave to remain made removal disproportionate
Internal relocation to Kinshasa safety
Whether 2004 Home Office family concession policy assisted the appellant
linked_authorities: Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 105
Mahmood v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] INLR 1
Jakupovic v Austria (2004) 38 EHRR 27

notes: Split Court of Appeal on Cathay Pacific pilots' ERA jurisdiction after Serco; Veta pilots remitted.

enrichment.short_title: Crofts v Cathay Pacific: ERA jurisdiction for overseas-based airline pilots
key_facts: British-resident Cathay Pacific pilots employed by Hong Kong shell companies Veta and USAB claimed unfair dismissal and breach of contract after dismissal in Hong Kong.
Veta pilots were based at London Heathrow though contracts, pay, training and management were Hong Kong-centred.
Section 196 ERA was repealed in 1999; Lawson v Serco held Part X applies to employment in Great Britain.
Majority held international airline pilots fall outside Serco; minority remitted Veta pilots' ERA claims as borderline.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeals on employment tribunal jurisdiction for unfair dismissal and wrongful dismissal after EAT decisions post-Serco.
enrichment.outcome: Split court: MRR dismissed Veta pilots' ERA appeal and stayed contract claims; Waller and Maurice Kay LJJ allowed Veta pilots' ERA appeal and remitted; CPA pilots and Parrock appeals dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: After repeal of section 196 and per Serco, section 94(1) protects employment in Great Britain with flexible assessment of where work is based; the majority held international airline pilots generally lack a terrestrial place of employment in Great Britain, while the minority applied Todd-style base analysis to Veta pilots based at Heathrow.
legal_issues: Territorial scope of Part X ERA after repeal of section 196
Meaning of employment in Great Britain under Serco for mobile airline pilots
Employment tribunal jurisdiction over Hong Kong contract claims
Forum non conveniens and stay of breach of contract claims
linked_authorities: Lawson v Serco Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 12
Todd v British Midland Airways [1978] ICR 959
Carver v Saudi Arabian Airlines [1999] ICR 991

notes: Clinical negligence trial; failure to read post-operative x-rays caused delayed revision surgery and foot drop.

enrichment.short_title: Leake v Targett: negligent failure to detect spinal cage slippage
key_facts: Mr Leake underwent instrumented lumbar spinal fusion by Mr Targett in March 2000 and developed post-operative leg numbness.
The defendant failed to notice intervertebral cage slippage on March x-rays, told the patient all was fine, and discharged him without monitoring.
Revision surgery in August 2000 was difficult and left permanent left foot drop; agreed damages were £60,000 if liable.
Experts agreed early revision before end of April 2000 would probably have avoided foot drop.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of liability in clinical negligence concerning post-operative care after spinal fusion surgery.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant in the agreed sum of £60,000; the defendant negligently misread x-rays and delay caused avoidable foot drop.
enrichment.ratio: A surgeon who negligently fails to detect cage prolapse on post-operative x-rays and adopts a wait-and-see policy without monitoring breaches duty of care; on the balance of probabilities competent interpretation would have led to early revision surgery avoiding permanent foot drop.
legal_issues: Whether the defendant noticed cage slippage on March 2000 x-rays
Appropriate management after detected or undetected cage movement
Causation between delayed revision and foot drop
Standard of post-operative monitoring and patient communication

confidence.notes: Detailed factual findings on x-ray misreading and expert consensus on causation are explicit.

notes: Clinical negligence appeal dismissed; anaesthetist should have suspected atracurium reaction after bronchospasm.

enrichment.short_title: Eastwood v Wright: failure to investigate anaesthetic bronchospasm
key_facts: Mrs Wright suffered acute bronchospasm at induction of anaesthesia using atracurium during a 1995 hysterectomy performed by Dr Eastwood.
The anaesthetist treated the spasm with aminophylline and diagnosed smoking-related irritation rather than adverse drug reaction.
In 1999 she suffered life-changing anaphylaxis to cisatracurium during another operation; experts agreed prior suspicion would have prevented use of related drugs.
A 1979 record noted possible althesin allergy; 1990 AAGBI guidance required full investigation of suspected anaphylactic reactions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from deputy High Court judge's liability finding after trial on anaesthetic negligence and causation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to find reasonable suspicion of adverse drug reaction requiring investigation and warning.
enrichment.ratio: Where intense peri-induction bronchospasm in a non-asthmatic patient required aminophylline, a responsible anaesthetist by 1995 should have suspected adverse drug reaction and complied with AAGBI guidance to investigate and warn, irrespective of whether bronchospasm occurred strictly before or after intubation.
legal_issues: Whether bronchospasm occurred pre- or post-intubation
Whether aminophylline use indicated severity supporting drug reaction suspicion
Application of 1990 AAGBI anaphylaxis guidance
Causation link to 1999 cisatracurium anaphylaxis

confidence.notes: Expert agreement on causation and detailed appellate review of fact findings support high confidence.

notes: EU public policy deportation appeal allowed; IAT failed to assess present threat and proportionality.

enrichment.short_title: Machado v SSHD: EEA deportation and public policy proportionality
key_facts: Angolan national Mr Machado committed benefit fraud exceeding £8,000 and motoring offences; he married a British woman who later acquired Irish citizenship.
The Home Secretary decided to remove him as family member of an EEA national on public policy grounds after serving a prison sentence.
The marriage was accepted as genuine; the IAT focused on past conduct and immigration history rather than present threat.
A probation officer reported low risk of reoffending after supervised licence period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on lawfulness of IAT upholding deportation under EEA Regulations and Article 8 after fraud convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a differently constituted IAT for proper assessment of present public policy threat and proportionality.
enrichment.ratio: Deportation of a non-EEA spouse under the 2000 Regulations requires conduct posing a real and sufficiently serious present threat to a fundamental social interest and proportionate removal; tribunals must not conflate public policy with general immigration policy, dismiss probation evidence without sound reasons, or rely on manipulative acquisition of rights to dilute protection.
legal_issues: Correct public policy test under regulations 21 and 23 and Directive 64/221/EEC
Whether ex post facto Home Office reasons could justify deportation
Integration of Article 8 proportionality with EEA removal decision
Present threat requirement per Orfanopoulos
linked_authorities: Carpenter v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 2 WLR 267
Orfanopoulos v Land Baden-Wuerttemberg [2005] 1 CMLR 18
Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 105
